routes.description: Establish that agency and rational normativity cannot be reduced to causal compulsion, then use Bradleyan idealism to place lawful explanation within a wider experiential reality.
routes.successCriteria: Show that determinist inference does not eliminate agential sourcehood or relevant modal alternatives and that idealism integrates domains that reductive naturalism leaves unexplained.

motionBridge.description: Libertarian idealism must preserve meaningful agency under lawful description while providing a more comprehensive account of experience than naturalistic reduction.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish mathematical or logical determination from causal compulsion and explain why the former need not displace agents as sources.
Supply an account of alternative possibility and sourcehood that does not depend upon a presently branching physical timeline.
Show why scientific representation is one mode within experience rather than an exhaustive inventory of reality.
Explain how truth, value, feeling, and inquiry can be integrated without reducing them to abstract thought alone.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect indispensable responsibility practices to a real distinction between agency and mere bodily occurrence.
Identify experiential, practical, and intellectual constraints that prevent idealism from collapsing into arbitrary invention.

routes.description: Maintain determinist pressure on libertarian alternatives while reconstructing freedom and inquiry through their practical functions without requiring Bradleyan metaphysics.
routes.successCriteria: Show that changing causal vocabulary or modal scope does not secure libertarian freedom, and that pragmatic standards preserve responsibility and disciplined inquiry more economically.

motionBridge.description: Compatibilist pragmatism must retain action-guiding freedom and standards of inquiry while showing that libertarian idealism adds no necessary explanatory gain.

centralBridges.description: Establish that fixed laws and states threaten genuine alternatives even when the determining relation is described as non-causal.
Test whether varying pasts or laws answers the fixed-premise consequence challenge or merely changes the relevant possible worlds.
Explain freedom through the practical distinctions needed for incentives, responsibility, praise, and blame under determinism.
Provide disciplined pragmatic standards for experience-centered inquiry without committing to a substantially existent absolute.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish perspectival or mind-framed access to reality from voluntary construction or mind-controlled truth.
Retain methodological pluralism while specifying constraints that exclude both scientistic reduction and unrestricted inclusion.

sections.title: Determinism, causation, and agential sourcehood
sections.rationale: This issue contains the motion's primary clash over whether complete lawful determination amounts to causal constraint and whether agency can remain explanatorily fundamental.

sections.title: Alternative possibilities and the consequence argument
sections.rationale: The modal scope of doing otherwise determines whether libertarian freedom survives a fixed timeline and whether sourcehood can be separated from control over past facts and laws.

sections.title: Practical responsibility and metaphysical agency
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether freedom's indispensable social functions are sufficient for compatibilism or instead presuppose a deeper distinction between genuine action and bodily occurrence.

sections.title: Experience, science, and naturalistic reduction
sections.rationale: The comparative metaphysical burden turns on whether science exhausts reality, whether other experiential domains require systematic inclusion, and whether a restrained naturalistic idealism can include experience.

sections.title: The absolute and the completion of inquiry
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether Bradleyan integration names a real completion that grounds inquiry or only an aspirational ideal whose substantial existence remains unestablished.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Agency is needed to make sense of practical life, while objections to libertarian agency rely on contestable physicalist and causal-closure assumptions.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley directly asks Hawkins about his libertarian position, and the uninterrupted answer is delivered in Hawkins's first-person voice.

response.rationale: This constructive opening establishes the debate's agency problem and challenges the physicalist and causal-closure assumptions said to support determinism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly opens the central agency route, though the positive libertarian account remains largely prospective.

precisionFindings.rationale: The practical indispensability claim and qualified contrast with compatibilism are recoverable, but agency and the challenged closure assumptions remain incompletely specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents agency as needed for practical explanation while expressly conceding that compatibilism supplies much of what is required.

charity.alternative: Compatibilism may preserve most practically important agency without libertarian alternatives.
charity.decisiveQualification: The speaker expressly grants this practical success before claiming that a further aspect of free will remains.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The practical-life premise supports retaining agency, but it does not alone establish specifically libertarian sourcehood.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Practical indispensability supplies a relevant consideration, while the objections' disputed assumptions are mostly asserted here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly introduces the central requirement that lawful description not eliminate agents as sources.

representationalCharity.rationale: The live compatibilist alternative is stated as substantially successful rather than weakened for convenience.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes everyday and philosophical explanatory practice, concedes compatibilism's reach, and identifies an additional free-will concern.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Complete knowledge of particle states and natural laws appears sufficient to derive every later event, excluding genuine alternatives.
moves.attributionBasis: The host explicitly frames his naturalist audience's inherited determinist argument and then asks Hawkins where that reasoning fails.

components.text: Whether contestable causal-closure assumptions genuinely leave room for libertarian alternatives.
Whether practical reliance on agency establishes more than a useful compatibilist notion.

response.rationale: The Laplacean derivability challenge directly contests the proposed opening for libertarian alternatives, but it does not address the separate argument from practical indispensability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It sharply contacts the decisive metaphysical component while leaving the practical component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The fixed-state-and-laws challenge and its target are clear, although the idealizations governing complete knowledge and derivability remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move frames derivability as an apparent consequence and asks where it fails, but compresses the bridge from predictability to lack of alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Fixed complete states and laws intelligibly support unique evolution, though derivability and agential impossibility are not identical.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Laplacean model is a relevant thought experiment, but its physical and modal premises are not independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central determinist bridge concerning fixed laws, states, and genuine alternatives.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move poses the standard determinist challenge without materially reconstructing a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt specifies complete particle positions, all natural laws, derivation of subsequent events, and the resulting challenge to doing otherwise.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Mathematical determination in theoretical physics is non-causal, whereas experimental causation is intervention-based and rooted in an agential perspective.
moves.attributionBasis: After Folley asks which concepts of causation support determinism, Hawkins explicitly invokes his idealist approach and delivers the extended answer.

components.text: Whether complete lawful derivability is itself a causal relation that excludes agential sourcehood.
Whether unique derivability excludes genuine alternative possibilities even if the relation is non-causal.

response.rationale: The answer distinguishes truth-functional determination from intervention-based causation and locates the latter in agency, but does not yet show how alternatives survive unique determination.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a developed answer to the causal component while leaving the distinct modal component unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The theoretical-versus-experimental distinction is clear, but causation shifts between scientific methodology and metaphysical dependence without a fully explicit bridge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The truth-functional characterization is asserted confidently and supported by a useful contrast, though its applicability to every determinist relation is not shown.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction blocks an immediate equation of determination with causation, but does not itself secure sourcehood under fixed evolution.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The contrast between theoretical relations and experimental interventions is apt, though the metaphysical conclusion needs further warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central agency bridge by separating mathematical determination from causal compulsion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own distinction rather than relying on a consequential representation of a live alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls theoretical determination a truth-functional relation and contrasts it with experimental manipulation using control and intervention.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Even non-causal determination threatens libertarian freedom when fixed laws and states exclude genuinely branching alternative futures.
moves.attributionBasis: The host addresses Hawkins's preceding distinction, articulates a determinist audience's objection, and ends by posing two alternatives to Hawkins.

components.text: Whether non-causal but fixed determination still excludes genuinely branching alternative futures.
Whether intervention-based causation establishes agents as metaphysically fundamental sources.

response.rationale: The reply correctly isolates the modal threat that remains after causation is redescribed, while leaving the interventionist account of agency largely untouched.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It presses the decisive residual objection but does not answer the separate positive sourcehood proposal.

precisionFindings.rationale: The fixed-states, fixed-laws, and branching-futures issue is expressed clearly, with the objection explicitly limited to non-causal determination.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move says the branching picture still seems undermined and presents alternatives as questions rather than claiming a completed demonstration.

charity.alternative: Determination may be non-causal while experimental intervention supplies a genuine notion of agency.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even granting non-causal determination, fixed states and laws may still leave only one future.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The residual inference from fixed laws and states to a single branching future is clear and internally stable.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The fixed-state model supports the challenge, although the possibility-space assumptions are still not fully defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move squarely supports the central determination bridge after accommodating the opponent's causal distinction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the opponent's causal distinction and targets the remaining modal consequence rather than ignoring it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt holds laws and states fixed, invokes perfect prediction in both temporal directions, and argues that branching alternatives remain undermined.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Libertarian freedom need not require a presently branching timeline because sourcehood and the modal possibility of doing otherwise are separable ingredients.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly introduces his own libertarian position after contrasting it with branching-futures accounts, identifying the passage as Hawkins's answer.

components.text: Whether libertarian freedom necessarily requires multiple presently branching physical futures.
How sourcehood and doing otherwise can remain substantive under fixed non-causal determination.

response.rationale: The move rejects branching futures as a necessary condition and separates sourcehood from doing otherwise, but the excerpt does not yet supply a full account of either ingredient.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive assumption behind the objection, while its replacement account remains materially incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-component thesis is recoverable and carefully qualified, but sourcehood and the relevant sense of possibility are only introduced, not stabilized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker makes the bounded claim that libertarianism need not require branching futures and explicitly presents it as his own account.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Separating sourcehood and alternatives is coherent, but merely distinguishing them does not explain their compatibility with fixed evolution.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual proposal is relevant but largely programmatic, with its modal and sourcehood warrants still undeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central modality bridge by rejecting dependence on a presently branching timeline.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move distinguishes its view from branching accounts without a distortion on which its inference depends.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly denies that his libertarian position necessarily needs branching futures and identifies sourcehood and doing otherwise as distinct ingredients.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Allowing different pasts or laws changes the fixed premise rather than showing a different outcome with the actual past and laws held fixed.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is framed as a critical question and is immediately followed by Hawkins's marked explanatory answer, matching Folley's role in the dialogue.

components.text: Whether alternatives obtained by varying the past or laws answer a challenge that fixes both.
Whether sourcehood can be established independently of control over prior facts and laws.

response.rationale: The question precisely challenges the modal scope of doing otherwise, but it does not engage the proposed independence of sourcehood from alternative possibilities.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It targets the decisive modal component clearly while leaving the separate sourcehood component open.

precisionFindings.rationale: The notation fixes past facts and laws as P and the decision as Q, making the difference between fixed-premise and varied-premise worlds explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker poses a focused objection and openly signals uncertainty rather than claiming that the challenge has already been proved.

charity.alternative: Doing otherwise may be evaluated across worlds whose past facts or laws differ from the actual world.
charity.decisiveQualification: That modal scope does not by itself answer the consequence argument's fixed-P question.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between varying P and holding P fixed is crisp and exposes a genuine mismatch in modal questions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The formalized P-to-Q comparison adequately supports the conceptual objection, with little empirical support required.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central consequence bridge by testing whether changing premises answers the fixed-premise challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The alternative is reconstructed in a strong form before the exact scope mismatch is identified.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly defines P as past facts plus natural laws, Q as the decision, and contrasts fixed-P with different-P counterfactuals.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: The consequence argument conflates logical dependence with agential dependence when it transfers lack of control over past facts into lack of control over present acts.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage directly answers Folley's question, develops Hawkins's first-person idealist account of agency, and ends before Folley's next marked intervention.

components.text: Whether lack of control over fixed past facts validly transfers through logical dependence to lack of control over present action.
Whether the opponent's broader modal scope directly supplies an alternative outcome with actual past and laws fixed.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the transfer principle as conflating logical connection with agential dependence and explains why fixed-premise control need not propagate through implication.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly attacks the objection's inferential engine, though it does not construct a fixed-P alternative outcome.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alleged transfer from not controlling P to not sourcing or controlling Q is clearly stated, distinguished from logical implication, and assigned a specific consequence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conflation diagnosis is forceful and intelligible, but the excerpt does not fully establish that every consequence argument depends on the disputed transfer.

charity.alternative: If P entails Q and an agent has no control over P, the absence of control may transfer to Q.
charity.decisiveQualification: Logical entailment alone does not establish that sourcehood or control follows the same dependence relation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The logical-versus-agential dependence distinction is a coherent diagnostic challenge to the transfer inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is relevant, but a positive account showing independent sourcehood would strengthen the defeating consequence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central consequence bridge by challenging the transfer from fixed past to present control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opposing transfer principle is stated in recognizable strong form before its agential premise is challenged.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states the inference from no sourcehood or control over P to none over Q and argues that logical relations do not carry agential relations automatically.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: The competing accounts may quantify over different possible worlds, leaving the fixed-past challenge unresolved rather than substantively rebutted.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage follows Hawkins's extended answer as a skeptical reformulation and is followed by Hawkins's marked response, clearly identifying Folley as speaker.

components.text: Whether the dispute is resolved by distinguishing agential dependence from logical dependence.
Whether the competing positions instead quantify over materially different sets of possible worlds.

response.rationale: The reply reframes the exchange as a scope difference between variable-past and fixed-past worlds, preserving the fixed-premise objection despite the dependence distinction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It engages the core diagnosis and identifies a precise residual disagreement about modal scope.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two quantificational scopes are clearly contrasted, and the speaker expressly allows that the broader scope is legitimate while denying equivalence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move cautiously presents a scope diagnosis and qualifies it by acknowledging the legitimacy of the opponent's alternative modal question.

charity.alternative: Alternative possibility can legitimately range over worlds where the past and future both differ.
charity.decisiveQualification: That legitimate scope is distinct from asking what worlds remain when the past and natural laws are fixed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The competing-domain analysis is clear and shows why the earlier diagnostic need not settle the fixed-past challenge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The explicit possible-worlds comparison provides strong conceptual support, with only the choice of privileged scope left open.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the consequence bridge by distinguishing variable-premise from fixed-premise modal evaluation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opponent's scope is explicitly described as legitimate before its non-equivalence to the fixed scope is argued.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts quantification over worlds with alterable pasts and futures against worlds constrained by the same past and laws.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: A pragmatically indispensable notion of freedom survives complete determinism because societies must distinguish conduct that incentives can influence from conduct they cannot.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person account follows Hawkins's response, names Folley's compatibilism, and belongs to Folley's clearly marked conversational turn.

response.rationale: This constructive move argues that determinist societies retain a practically necessary freedom distinction by tracking which conduct responds to incentives and disincentives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It establishes a clear functional compatibilist route, although its sufficiency against libertarian demands remains to be shown.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed minimal freedom concept, deterministic setting, and incentive-sensitive behavioral distinction are all explicit and consistently scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The practical need for behavioral sorting is strongly motivated, but the claim that every deterministic society must adopt this particular freedom concept is not fully established.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The need to distinguish incentive-responsive conduct coherently supports a minimal action-guiding conception of freedom.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The social-function thought experiment is apt, though it remains illustrative rather than comparative or empirically documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central compatibilist-function bridge through incentives under complete determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive functional account does not depend on a material representation of an opposing developed position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt imagines a deterministic society that must sort behavior for which incentives are sensible from behavior for which they are not.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Freedom should be analyzed through the functions of praise, blame, and incentives rather than assumed to possess a single metaphysical essence.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn continues Folley's first-person examples and explicitly develops the compatibilist analysis introduced earlier in his speech.

response.rationale: This constructive continuation proposes analyzing freedom through what it does—especially proportioning praise, blame, and incentives—rather than positing one metaphysical essence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies a clear methodological and functional account, while the completeness of that account remains contestable.

precisionFindings.rationale: The functional question, analogy with truth analysis, and identified roles of freedom are explicit and retain a stable practical scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker claims there is room for a functional analysis and offers concrete functions, avoiding the stronger claim that all metaphysical questions are thereby dissolved.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Moving from identifiable social functions to a functional analysis is coherent, though it does not prove metaphysical questions dispensable.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Praise, blame, and incentive practices provide relevant support, but the analogy to truth analysis remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly develops the central bridge explaining freedom by its responsibility and incentive functions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances a positive methodological proposal without a consequential reconstruction of the opposing view.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly asks what free will does and identifies its role in proportioning incentives, praise, and blame.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Even a deterministic society must retain a metaphysical distinction between agency and mere bodily occurrence because practical and moral life depend upon it.
moves.attributionBasis: A marked speaker transition begins the response, and Hawkins explicitly takes up the examples and functional claims from Folley's preceding turn.

components.text: Whether the practical functions of freedom require a real distinction between action and mere bodily occurrence.
Whether a deterministic society can preserve incentive-sensitive behavioral sorting without libertarian metaphysics.
Whether functional analysis alone is sufficient without a metaphysical essence of agency.

response.rationale: The reply accepts the practical examples but argues they presuppose a distinction between agency and spasmodic occurrence; it does not show why that distinction must be libertarian.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the shared practical core strongly while leaving the compatibilist sufficiency claim incompletely answered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The action-versus-spasm distinction is clear, but calling it metaphysical does not specify which properties exceed the compatibilist functional distinction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The inability to live without some agency distinction is plausible, but it does not establish that the distinction must include libertarian sourcehood.

charity.alternative: Compatibilism can distinguish deliberate punching from an involuntary muscle spasm by their functional and causal profiles.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply treats the practical distinction as requiring genuine agency but does not show why functional profiles are insufficient.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Practical distinctions support some agency concept, but the inference to a specifically metaphysical or libertarian distinction is underargued.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The punch-versus-spasm example is relevant, yet it cannot by itself decide between compatibilist and libertarian explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly supports the subsidiary practice bridge by tying responsibility practices to an agency-occurrence distinction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opponent's example is retained, but its compatibilist explanatory resources are materially compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that social life cannot discard free will because it must distinguish intentional punching from an involuntary muscle spasm.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Bradleyan idealism accepts scientific truths while rejecting the additional naturalist assumption that those truths exhaust everything real or experientially significant.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly invites Hawkins to explain Bradley, and the marked response is a long first-person exposition consistent with Hawkins's stated Bradleyan commitments.

response.rationale: This constructive move accepts scientific explanation while challenging the separate exclusivity premise that scientific truths exhaust reality and experience.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies a clear central idealist distinction, though the positive integration of additional domains remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: Scientific truth and the additional 'nothing else' assumption are cleanly separated, with the rejection directed at exhaustiveness rather than science itself.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The historical-expository claim is forceful, but the central argumentative point is modest: scientific accounts do not logically contain their own exhaustiveness premise.

charity.alternative: Naturalism can accept scientific truths and add the thesis that no other truths or realities are needed.
charity.decisiveQualification: The exclusivity thesis is an additional assumption rather than a result supplied by the scientific truths themselves.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Separating scientific results from an added exhaustiveness thesis is valid and blocks an immediate inference to reductionism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual separation is well supported, though showing that additional realities exist requires further positive evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central idealism bridge by denying that scientific representation exhausts reality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The naturalist position is represented as science plus an explicit closure thesis, not as rejection of experience or science.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt affirms scientific truths, identifies the added claim that there are no other truths, and attributes its rejection to Bradleyan idealism.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Direct feeling and volitional agency precede intellectual systematization, so scientific representation is only one mode of access to reality.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Hawkins's extended answer and explicitly contrasts Bradley's view with Hegel's thought-centered idealism.

response.rationale: This constructive move argues that feeling and volition are modes of engagement with reality prior to reflective and scientific representation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expands the experiential basis of idealism, though priority in experience does not by itself establish metaphysical priority.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast among feeling, volition, and thought is recoverable, but 'ground floor' priority moves between phenomenological and ontological senses.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The rejection of thought as exhaustive is supported by the experiential contrast, while the claim of precedence needs a clearer sense of priority.

charity.alternative: Hegelian idealism identifies reality with rational structure or thought.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bradley's alternative includes rational structure but denies that thought exhausts feeling, volition, and agency.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple modes of engagement support non-exhaustiveness, but experiential precedence does not automatically establish ontological precedence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Feeling and volition are relevant experiential data, though the broader metaphysical conclusion remains only partly warranted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central idealism bridge by presenting science and thought as non-exhaustive modes.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opposing rationalist thesis is stated recognizably and answered through an inclusive rather than merely contrary account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that reality includes feeling, volition, and agency, rejects identification of the real with the rational, and places thought after direct engagement.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: A naturalistically acceptable idealism can treat experience as inquiry's subject matter and physical objects as constructed models without positing a mysterious mental substance.
moves.attributionBasis: A marked transition follows Hawkins addressing Joe, and the speaker's first-person Humean and Carnapian commitments identify the turn as Folley's.

components.text: Whether experience-centered inquiry requires realities beyond naturalistically acceptable models.
Whether treating experience as primary can be distinguished from positing mysterious mental substance.
Whether science includes an undefended exhaustiveness clause.

response.rationale: The reply offers a naturalistic idealism that centers experience and treats objects as models, answering the demand for inclusion without directly defending scientific exhaustiveness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the central positive motivation for idealism, while leaving the closure-premise criticism unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The naturalistic alternative is recoverable and expressly disavows mysterious mental stuff, though 'constructed models' remains metaphysically underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents the view as a naturalistically acceptable possibility and carefully distinguishes it from a strong mental-substance ontology.

charity.alternative: Idealism may claim that reality includes experience, feeling, and thought rather than only physical descriptions.
charity.decisiveQualification: This insight can be retained by treating experience as inquiry's target without positing mental substance or a Bradleyan absolute.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed middle position coherently separates experience-centered inquiry from a mental-substance ontology.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Humean and Carnapian model is plausible, but standards constraining model construction are not supplied in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central inquiry bridge by offering experience-centered naturalism without a substantial absolute.

representationalCharity.rationale: The experiential motivation is preserved while a more economical metaphysical interpretation is proposed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts mysterious mental stuff with making sense of experience through naturalistically acceptable idealism and constructed physical models.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Although reflective subjects cannot recover wholly precognitive experience, unbounded feeling is ultimately integrated with complete structure, value, and agency in the absolute.
moves.attributionBasis: Hawkins explicitly turns to Folley's remaining question and gives a continuous Bradleyan answer until Folley introduces a comparison with Peirce.

components.text: Whether experience-centered naturalistic modeling can integrate feeling, structure, value, and agency without an absolute.
Whether positing the absolute adds more than a mysterious metaphysical substance.

response.rationale: The reply describes the absolute as an integration of all feeling, structural understanding, moral history, and agency, but does not directly justify its necessity over the naturalistic alternative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies issue-bearing positive integration and contacts one demand, while the comparative necessity question remains unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The integrative proposition is recoverable, but 'absolute,' completion, consciousness, and the end-of-time scope remain only partly delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that all experience, structure, value, and agency must unite in the absolute substantially exceeds the explanatory support supplied here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Integration is intelligible as a systematic aim, but the inference from partial domains to one completed absolute is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move describes Bradley's doctrine clearly but supplies little independent warrant for existence, necessity, or attainability.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central absolute bridge by integrating feeling, truth, value, structure, and agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mainly expounds the Bradleyan positive view and does not materially characterize the opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says every conscious feeling unites with complete structural and moral-volitional understanding in the absolute, where truth, goodness, and beauty are attained.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: The Bradleyan absolute may function only as a regulative ideal of completed inquiry, leaving its substantial existence or attainability unsettled.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly frames the comparison with C. S. Peirce, contrasts possible interpretations, and asks how certain Bradley is about the absolute's existence.

components.text: Whether the absolute is substantially existent rather than merely a regulative ideal of completed inquiry.
Whether complete integration is attainable by finite or future inquiry.

response.rationale: The reply directly tests both ontological commitment and attainability by contrasting a substantial absolute with a Peircean end-of-inquiry ideal.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts the decisive existence claim and its closely related attainability component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between an existent absolute and an agnostic regulative endpoint is explicit, as is the separate question whether inquiry ever reaches it.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move carefully poses alternatives and acknowledges Peircean agnosticism without pretending that the ontological issue is already settled.

charity.alternative: Bradley's absolute is a real completed integration toward which inquiry is directed.
charity.decisiveQualification: Normative direction can instead be interpreted as a regulative ideal without establishing substantial existence or eventual attainment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regulative-versus-substantial distinction is clear and exposes a genuine unsupported step in the preceding account.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Peircean comparison strongly motivates the underdetermination, although it does not itself disprove Bradley's ontology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central absolute bridge by questioning existence and attainability rather than integration's description.

representationalCharity.rationale: The substantial interpretation is explicitly considered before the weaker and philosophically serious regulative alternative is raised.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts an existent absolute with Peircean agnosticism about perfect theory or inquiry's endpoint and asks how firmly Bradley asserts existence.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: The absolute is not merely a settled theory because inquiry's normative orientation toward completion recognizes a reality fuller than present partial understanding.
moves.attributionBasis: The pro speaker labels Folley's question, states Bradley's lack of agnosticism, and gives reasons before Folley begins a practical analogy.

components.text: Whether inquiry's normative orientation supplies reason to treat the complete whole as more than a regulative ideal.
Whether the absolute substantially exists independently of eventual human attainment.
Whether inquiry will or can actually attain the absolute.

response.rationale: The reply argues that normative orientation toward completion recognizes a fuller reality, but it leaves the existence inference underdefended and does not answer attainability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the central regulative challenge, while two decisive ontological and attainability components remain unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument from normative aiming to fuller reality is recoverable, but 'more real' and the relation between completion and existence remain unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move treats normative pursuit as recognition of greater reality, but direction toward an ideal does not by itself establish that ideal's substantial existence.

charity.alternative: The completed whole may regulate inquiry without existing as a substantially real achieved state.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply appeals to inquiry's normative drive but does not independently bridge normative orientation to ontology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move identifies a normative orientation, but the inference from aiming at completion to recognizing greater reality is incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Inquiry's pursuit of truth supports a regulative endpoint more readily than the asserted substantial Bradleyan absolute.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central absolute bridge by defending completion as fuller reality rather than merely settled theory.
